extracted.intended_audience: scientists, navigators, and magnetic-observatory observers and instrument-makers; educated public interested in terrestrial magnetism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical criteria for observing, measuring, mapping, and interpreting terrestrial magnetism (declination, inclination, and intensity), including instrument requirements, networked observatories, temporal/spectral sampling, and data standardization. Drawn from 19th-century observational practice and theory as described by Humboldt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map declination and isogonic lines; follow secular change
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the distribution of magnetic declination over the Earth's surface (isogonic lines) and monitor their secular change of configuration over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt describes closed oval systems of isogonic lines, regional peculiarities (e.g., northern Asia, South Sea), and the importance of following their progress over centuries to understand physical causes. Use historical records and repeated surveys (examples: Gilbert 1600, Columbus-era observations, Sabine's charts for 1825 vs 1837) to detect shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure horary (diurnal) variations of declination
rubrics_metrics.description: Record hour-by-hour variations in declination (horary variations) which are apparently governed by the Sun while above the horizon and vary with magnetic latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values diminish with magnetic latitude (e.g., 3–4' near equator, 13–14' in middle Europe). Seek the 'line of no motion' (region between terrestrial and magnetic equator with no horary deviations). High-frequency sampling across the day is required to characterize these variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the magnetic equator and its nodes; track nodal motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate the curve/line where the inclination of the needle is null (magnetic equator), identify its intersections with the terrestrial equator (nodes), and measure their secular displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observational crossings (e.g., Duperrey's six crossings 1822–1825) and repeat surveys (Sabine showed a 4° westward movement of a node between 1825 and 1837) to quantify nodal motion. Note that the magnetic equator traverses ocean and land and its oscillatory change influences inclination remotely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure inclination, declination, and intensity together (triple manifestation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and record the three principal magnetic quantities—declination, inclination, and intensity—since all three together characterize terrestrial magnetism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt emphasizes not to confound the physical science of magnetism with purely mathematical branches; perform simultaneous measurement of the triple manifestations to interpret spatial and temporal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine intensity via oscillation counts of needles and standardize to a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the intensity of the magnetic force by counting oscillations of a vertical or horizontal needle and reduce results to a chosen standard reference (Humboldt's unit on the magnetic equator in northern Peru).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt reports oscillation counts (e.g., same needle: 245 in Paris, 246 Havana, etc.) and derives relative intensity numbers (Paris = 1.3482 relative to Peruvian equator = 1.0000). Use the same needles or compare via calibration to ensure comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use delicate optical and chronometrical instruments for intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ sensitive optical and chronometrical apparatus to measure horizontal power (intensity) with a degree of accuracy exceeding other magnetic determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt cites instruments such as Prony's magnetic telescope, finely-divided scales, and carefully-suspended needles (thread devoid of torsion) with night illumination. Such precision permits detection of small fractional variations (example: 1/40000th of magnetic intensity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardize instruments and distribute similar apparatus with usage instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure comparability across stations by providing similar instruments and standard instructions for their use (as done by Gauss and Weber).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauss erected new principle apparatus and distributed instruments with instructions across Germany, Sweden, Italy. Standard instrumentation and procedure are essential to form a coherent network and to interpret simultaneous observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a network of magnetic observatories with broad geographic coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a net-work of magnetic stations across both hemispheres, spanning wide ranges of longitude and latitude, to detect global patterns and distinguish regional effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt advocated permanent stations in Canada, St. Helena, Cape of Good Hope, Isle of France, Ceylon, New Holland, and describes coverage from Toronto to Van Diemen's Land and from Paris to Pekin. Broad spatial coverage makes ocean-traversing features (magnetic equator) more accessible and allows mapping of isodynamic/isoclinic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make simultaneous observations at multiple observatories to separate local from global phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate observations at prearranged times among stations to determine whether perturbations are local or have global character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt recounts simultaneous observations between Berlin, Paris, Freiburg, and later many stations; simultaneous perturbations indicate general terrestrial phenomena. The magnetic association centered at Gottingen undertook such simultaneous 24-hour observations quarterly since 1836.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer continuous uninterrupted observations (observatio perpetua) over single occasional readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Carry out continuous, uninterrupted recordings for several days and nights rather than isolated single observations taken over many months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt and Oltmanns practiced hour-to-hour and half-hour-to-half-hour monitoring for multiple consecutive days to capture perturbations and periodicities; continuous records are better at revealing temporary storms and recurring disturbances than scattered single readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: High temporal resolution sampling (short sampling intervals and 24-hour coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Record observations at short time intervals (examples given: 2½ minutes at some observatories; hourly to sub-hourly elsewhere) and maintain continuous 24-hour series when feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes observations at intervals of 2½ minutes continued for 24 consecutive hours and other practices of frequent sampling to detect small and fast perturbations (magnetic storms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce comparative charts and maps to reveal secular changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Create isoclinic, isogonic, and isodynamic charts and compare maps across time (e.g., year-to-year or multi-year charts) to reveal secular motion and configuration changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt references Sabine's chart of isoclinic lines for 1825 and 1837 and stresses the value of graphical representation for the laws of terrestrial magnetism and detecting changes in node positions or oval systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify intensity variations with latitude using many observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish numerical relations of magnetic intensity across latitudes (e.g., intensity increases from equator toward poles) by aggregating many observations from different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt reports results from 104 places and cites comparative oscillation-derived intensities (e.g., unit 1.000 at Peruvian equator, Paris 1.3482, etc.). Large-sample comparisons underpin the law of intensity variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use identical needles where possible for comparative oscillation experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare oscillations of the same physical needles at different locations to minimize instrument-related variance when deducing differences in intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt describes moving the same needle among Paris, Havana, Mexico, St. Carlos del Rio Negro, Lima to get directly comparable oscillation counts; this practice reduces calibration uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and analyze magnetic perturbations (storms) via cross-station parallelism
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify magnetic storms and disturbances by their simultaneous or correlated appearance at multiple stations and by the parallelism of needle movements across observatories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include simultaneous perturbations observed in October–December 1829 and the Antarctic expedition's coordinated observations; such parallelism helps distinguish general terrestrial phenomena from local disturbances due to heat or cloudiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and test hypotheses about physical causes (solar, thermo-electric, planetary rotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate and evaluate hypotheses for the causes of periodical and secular magnetic phenomena (e.g., solar influence, thermo-electric currents, planetary rotation, internal currents) and design observations to test them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt discusses possibilities—thermo-magnetic currents (Seebeck), solar-induced currents, influence of planetary rotation, internal electro-dynamic currents as proposed by Ampere—and notes current inability to definitively assign causes, recommending broad, coordinated observation to provide evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce observational data to a common standard and document units/assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporting magnetic intensity and related measures, clearly state the unit and the reference standard used, and reduce local observations to that standard for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humboldt notes that many tables reduce oscillations to his chosen standard (magnetic equator in Northern Peru) and emphasizes the necessity to specify such arbitrary units so values (e.g., Paris = 1.348) are interpretable and comparable.
